newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Aluminum demand/price rebound on horizon.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Aluminum demand/price rebound on horizon.

text.p: After a dismal year for prices and demand, the aluminum industry is crossing its fingers that offtake will strengthen next year to mop up the extra metal set to hit the market.
Last December analysts expected 1996 tags to average about 99 cents per pound, a far cry from current levels.
LME cash settled Monday at the equivalent of 69 cents.
Some blamed copper's Sumitomo debacle for dragging down aluminum.
"The basic fundamentals are not as good as people expected. Sumitomo did not make LME inventories go up," Chuck Bradford of UBS Securities said.

Even so, based on global inventories, the price of aluminum should be about 80 cents per pound, Bradford said. "I think the corner was turned a few weeks ago and we will start to get some restocking in the beginning of next year."
CRU International's John Martin added, "The key issue next year is to what extent we get restocking along the pipeline."
Western world demand will have to grow about four percent - compared to about half a percent dip this year - to mop up the 350,000 tonnes or so of new capacity coming on stream in 1997, Martin said.
"There will probably be a balanced market or slight deficit next year with a modest increase in prices at best," Martin said. Growth of four percent was probable, he added.

Both UBS and MacQuarie Equities expected a small deficit of about 200,000 tonnes in 1997, the latter adding that its forecast of 4.1 percent growth next year could well turn out to be on the low side.
Analyst Jim Southwood of Commodity Metals Management said the biggest issue in 1997 will be how fast new smelter capacity in the Middle East and Asia starts up.
"They are coming on faster than even our estimations," Southwood said.
Russian aluminum exports, seen by many as an integral part of Western supply by now, were still a key factor.
"We think there is a big swing ahead in Russian exports to the downside," said analyst Dan Roling of Merrill Lynch. This will eat into LME aluminum stocks and push up prices, he added.

As for aluminium equities, Bradford said they were fairly priced but saw no bargains. "I still cannot find anything to buy but I think conditions are much better for next year," Bradford said. "If the metal price goes up, as I think it will, stocks will go up."

But aluminum producers who also produce large amounts of alumina will suffer next year. Alumina contracts were being settled at 11 to 11.2 percent of LME instead of 13 percent in 1996. "Alcoa is going to get bagged big time in alumina," Bradford said.

And Alcoa, along with Reynolds Metals and Alcan hold the key to unravelling hopes of a price hike, analysts said. The three companies have combined idled capacity of about 800,000 to 1 million tonnes.
"However, a premature restart would be enough to bring the market into balance or even into surplus, preventing prices from recovering," MacQuarie said.
Average price forecasts for 1997 in U.S. cents per pound:
UBS Securities 85
Prudential Securities 72
Everen Securities 75
Merrill Lynch 90
MacQuarie Equities 75.5
